summary: Defines extensions to BGP-4 so it can carry routing information for multiple network layer protocols, such as IPv6. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4760.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers used to share only one kind of address map. This lets them share maps for other kinds too, such as the newer address system.

questions: how does bgp carry ipv6 routes
subtitle: How BGP-4 learned to carry routes for IPv6 and other network protocols without breaking old routers.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 could only carry routing information for IPv4, because its next hop, aggregator and prefix information are all IPv4 specific.
tldr.mechanism: Two new optional, non-transitive attributes, MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI, carry an address family, a next hop and prefixes for any network layer protocol. Routers announce support through BGP capabilities.
tldr.outcome: A router that supports the extensions can interoperate with one that does not. RFC 2858 obsoleted RFC 2283 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4760.

today: RFC 2858 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000. It obsoleted RFC 2283 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4760.

sections.title: Why BGP-4 Needed Extending
sections.content:
Only three pieces of information in BGP-4 are specific to IPv4: the NEXT_HOP attribute, the AGGREGATOR attribute and the NLRI, which is expressed as IPv4 address prefixes. The RFC assumes every BGP speaker still has an IPv4 address, which is used for AGGREGATOR among other things.

So only two things must be added: a way to tie a network layer protocol to the next hop information, and a way to tie it to the NLRI. Protocols are identified with an Address Family, as defined in RFC 1700.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers could only talk about one kind of street address. This RFC lets them talk about other kinds of addresses too.

sections.title: Two New Attributes
sections.content:
Reachable destinations only need a next hop, and unreachable ones do not, so the RFC groups each kind separately. MP_REACH_NLRI (type code 14) carries reachable destinations together with the next hop to use. MP_UNREACH_NLRI (type code 15) carries destinations being withdrawn.

Both attributes are optional and non-transitive. A BGP speaker that does not understand them ignores the information and does not pass it on to other speakers, which is what makes the extension backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: New routers use two special envelopes, one for good news and one for bad news. Old routers do not know what the envelopes mean, so they simply ignore them.

sections.title: Reach and Unreach Attribute Formats
sections.content:
MP_REACH_NLRI holds a 2-octet Address Family Identifier, a 1-octet Subsequent Address Family Identifier, the length and value of the next hop network address, a count of SNPAs (subnetwork points of attachment) with each one's length and value, and finally the NLRI. A count of 0 means no SNPAs are listed.

MP_UNREACH_NLRI is simpler: the AFI, the SAFI and a variable-length list of withdrawn routes. An UPDATE that carries it is not required to carry any other path attributes.

Each NLRI entry is a <length, prefix> pair. The length is one octet giving the prefix length in bits, and a length of zero matches all addresses of that family. The prefix is padded with trailing bits to an octet boundary, and the value of those bits is irrelevant.
sections.plainLanguage: Each envelope says what kind of address it is about, where to send traffic, and then lists the places. The cancel envelope just lists places that no longer work.

sections.title: Next Hops and UPDATE Rules
sections.content:
The next hop tells a router which border router to use for the listed destinations. A speaker may advertise its own interface address (a "first party" next hop) or another router's address ("third party"), as long as the external peer shares a common subnet with that address. Speakers must be able to disable third party next hops, for imperfectly bridged media or policy.

A speaker must never advertise a peer's address to that peer as the next hop for a route it originates, and must never install a route with itself as next hop. When advertising to an internal peer, it should not modify the next hop.

An UPDATE with MP_REACH_NLRI must also carry ORIGIN and AS_PATH, plus LOCAL_PREF in IBGP. From an external peer, if the leftmost AS in AS_PATH is not the peer's own AS number, the speaker sends a NOTIFICATION with Error Code UPDATE Message Error and subcode Malformed AS_PATH. If the UPDATE has no NLRI other than the multiprotocol one, it should not carry NEXT_HOP, and a receiver should ignore it if present.
sections.plainLanguage: The next hop is like saying which door to walk through to reach a place. Routers must never point a neighbor to a door that leads straight back to itself.

sections.title: SAFI Values and Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
The Subsequent Address Family Identifier says more about the NLRI. Three values are defined: 1 for unicast forwarding, 2 for multicast forwarding and 3 for both.

A speaker using these extensions should use BGP Capability Advertisement to learn whether a peer supports them. The Capability Code is 1, the length is 4, and the value is a 16-bit AFI, an 8-bit reserved field (set to 0 by the sender, ignored by the receiver) and an 8-bit SAFI. A speaker supporting several AFI/SAFI pairs lists each as a separate capability. For two-way exchange of a given pair, each speaker must advertise it to the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Before swapping maps, two routers say which kinds of maps they can read. They only trade the kinds both of them understand.

sections.title: Error Handling, IANA and Security
sections.content:
If an MP attribute is incorrect, the speaker must delete all routes received from that neighbor with the same AFI/SAFI, and should ignore later routes with that AFI/SAFI for the rest of the session. It may also end the session with the Notification "Update Message Error"/"Optional Attribute Error".

For IANA, SAFI 0 is reserved, 1 to 3 are assigned here, 4 to 63 use IETF Consensus, 64 to 127 use First Come First Served, and 128 to 255 are private use. On security, the RFC says the extension does not change the underlying security issues inherent in BGP.
sections.plainLanguage: If one kind of map from a neighbor is broken, a router throws away just that kind and stops listening to it, but keeps using the rest.
